text.p: Following are the leading stories in the Pakistani press on Sunday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- The International Monetary Fund has agreed to consider Pakistan's request to expand the $600 million stand-by arrangement and extend it to September next year. Pakistani officials said they hoped the blocked tranches of $160 million would be released by Thursday.
- The government has decided to formulate a new national food policy to achieve self-reliance and sufficiency.
- President Farooq Leghari claimed that ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto was not enjoying the support or the confidence of a majority in the National Assembly (lower house).

- The Supreme Court deferred hearing Benazir Bhutto's petition against the dissolution of the National Assembly and dismissal of her government till the disposal of other petitions challenging the presidential power to dissolve the assembly.
- Banks and development finance institutions have written off loans worth 6.31 billion rupees in the last five years.
- The management of Pakistan Telecommunication Company Ltd will be restructured to cut costs, said chairman Nasim Mirza.
- President Leghari said the Intelligence Bureau, working under the control of deposed prime minister Benazir Bhutto, had tapped the phones of judges, politicians and military officers.
- Business activity in Karachi was badly affected by a strike called by religious zealots protesting at the induction of an Ahmadi as a minister in the Sindh provincial cabinet.
- The state-run Trading Corporation of Pakistan has scrapped bids for the import of 50,000 tonnes of crystal white sugar and invited fresh tenders by December 21.
